title: Structural Units in Biochemistry and Genetics
subject: Biochemistry & genetics
summary: Structural units are the basic building blocks of cellular and tissue architecture, from nucleosomes to spectrin tetramers and liver lobules. Understanding their composition and dysfunction helps diagnose and manage common tropical diseases.

sections.p: Structural units are defined arrangements of macromolecules that give cells and organs their shape and mechanical properties. They range from the nucleosome in chromatin to the spectrin tetramer that supports red cell membranes, to the hexagonal lobule of the liver.
b: Nucleosome: DNA wrapped around histone octamer
Spectrin tetramer: α‑β heterodimers forming a flexible lattice
Liver lobule: hexagonal unit with central vein and portal triad

sections.p: Each unit is assembled by specific protein–protein or protein–DNA interactions. The nucleosome compacts DNA; spectrin tetramers provide shear resistance; the lobule organizes hepatic microcirculation.
b: DNA–histone binding creates 147 bp nucleosome core
α‑β spectrin dimerization via CH1/CH2 domains
Portal triad supplies bile, arterial and portal blood to acinus

t.b: Assess red cell morphology; spherocytes suggest spectrin defect
Detect lobular architecture changes; focal lesions may alter lobule shape

sections.p: Assembly is controlled by chaperones, post‑translational modifications and gene expression. Mutations or deficiencies in these regulators lead to structural instability.
b: Heat shock proteins assist spectrin folding
Cytokines influence hepatocyte proliferation within lobules

sections.p: Defects in structural units manifest as mechanical fragility, impaired DNA packaging, or altered organ perfusion. Tropical infections can target these units directly or indirectly.
b: Sickle cell disease: β‑globin mutation alters hemoglobin, causing rigid cells
Malaria: parasite invades erythrocytes, disrupting spectrin network
Schistosomiasis: egg deposition damages hepatic lobules

t.b: Identify sickle hemoglobin S; confirms hemoglobinopathy
Elevated in chronic inflammation; may mask iron deficiency

sections.p: Recognising structural unit pathology guides diagnosis, treatment choice and prognosis. In low‑resource settings, bedside clues and simple tests are vital.
b: Red cell shape on smear indicates spectrin or membrane protein defects
Liver function tests plus ultrasound suggest lobular damage

t.b: Low MCV may hint at thalassemia; high RDW suggests anisocytosis
High ratio (>2) points to alcoholic liver disease; low ratio suggests viral hepatitis

sections.p: Examiners test integration of structural knowledge with clinical scenarios. Focus on diagnostic criteria, differential diagnosis, and first‑line management.
b: Ask about family history for hereditary hemolytic anemias
Use the Coombs test to differentiate immune vs non‑immune hemolysis
Remember that schistosomiasis can cause portal hypertension via fibrotic lobule changes

whenToSeekHelp: Severe haemolysis with jaundice and hypotension
Unexplained ascites or splenomegaly in a patient with liver disease
Sudden drop in hemoglobin with evidence of intravascular rupture

faq.a: A flexible lattice formed by two α‑β heterodimers that stabilises the red cell membrane.

faq.q: How does a nucleosome affect gene expression?
faq.a: DNA wrapped around histones limits access to transcription factors; acetylation loosens this structure.

faq.q: Why does malaria damage the spectrin network?
faq.a: The parasite remodels the host cell, inserting proteins that disrupt spectrin‑actin interactions, making the cell rigid and prone to splenic clearance.
